summary: Specifies an application-level protocol called the Remote User Telnet service. Any host implementing this service must follow the protocol. This RFC is historic.

eli5.summary: A set of rules for letting someone far away use a computer through a terminal. It is now only of historical interest.

subtitle: A way for hosts with limited resources to provide remote terminal access via a well-known port.

tldr.problem: Small hosts with limited functionality need a way to provide terminal access to remote users without running a full system executive.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC designates port 107 (153 octal) as a well-known service for User Telnet connections, using the standard Telnet protocol to give remote operators terminal-like access.
tldr.outcome: This is a historic RFC; it was an early approach to remote terminal services that has been superseded by modern methods.

today: RFC 818 is marked Historic. It was an early mechanism for providing terminal access to small hosts but has been superseded by modern remote access methods.

sections.title: The Remote User Telnet Service
sections.content:
RFC 818 specifies a service that allows a user to access limited hosts over a network using the Telnet protocol. This RFC was suggested by Mike Mulligan at BBN and addresses the case where a host has very limited functionality and no system executive—the command shell that a user would normally interact with.

The service is accessed by making a connection to port 107 (octal 153). Once connected, the standard Telnet protocol is used for the interaction, allowing a user to send commands and receive responses as if they were at the host's terminal.
sections.eli5: The RFC says: if you want to talk to a tiny computer far away, connect to port 107, and you can type just like you are sitting next to it.

sections.title: Why This Service Was Needed
sections.content:
In the early ARPANET and Internet, hosts used well-known ports and sockets to offer distinct services. The most common of these was the Server Telnet port, which connected users to a system executive like TOPS-20 EXEC or the Unix Shell.

However, some small hosts had very limited functionality and no executive at all. For these systems, designating specific well-known ports for specific applications made sense. This RFC standardizes such a port for what is called the Remote User Telnet service.
sections.eli5: Big computers have a special place you can call to talk to them. Little computers without such a place needed one too, so this RFC created a standard spot.

sections.title: Example: The BBN TC68K Terminal Concentrator
sections.content:
The RFC provides a detailed example: the TC68K, a terminal concentrator based on the Motorola MC68000 at Bolt Beranek and Newman. It had one network connection, sixteen RS232 terminal connections, and ran the Micro-Operating System (MOS) with IP, ICMP, TCP, and Telnet protocols.

The TC68K software included a user Telnet application for network access and a server Telnet for connecting non-network-aware devices. To test remote units, BBN connected a user Telnet back-to-back with a server Telnet using a Pseudo Teletype (PTY) device driver, allowing operators to appear as a local terminal to a remote TC68K and verify the network path was working.
sections.eli5: At BBN, they made a small box to route terminals to a network. To test if a far-away box worked, they sent Telnet through the network as if it were a local terminal.
